The hole reached its greatest extent for the year on September 18 at 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That’s about 90% as large as the largest ozone hole ever observed, which occurred on September 9, 2000. “The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” Newman said. The ozone depletion process begins when human-made compounds containing chlorine and bromine are released into the environment. Air currents carry the gases up into the stratosphere, where they’re broken down by ultraviolet radiation. The freed chlorine and bromine atoms interact with cloud particles in the Antarctic stratosphere to enable ozone destruction. The stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal stream of wind encircling Antarctica, plays a key role by corralling the frigid air necessary to produce polar stratospheric clouds.
